items.title: CoreWeave, Nebius, and Neoclouds Sink as Market Fear Index Closes in on ‘Extreme Fear’
items.summary: CoreWeave (CRWV) and Nebius Group (NBIS) are plunging as fears of an AI financing crisis spread across Wall Street. With CNN's Fear & Greed Index approaching "Extreme Fear," investors are questioning whether the neocloud business model can survive rising borrowing costs. In this episode, 24/7 Wall St.'s Eric Bleeker breaks down why CoreWeave and Nebius have fallen more than 20% since October 8, and whether the sell-off represents a buying opportunity or a warning of deeper problems ahead. CoreWeave's unsecured bonds recently reached a 15% yield, raising concerns about its massive debt burden and ability to finance future expansion. Investor Chamath Palihapitiya has warned of a potential AI private credit bubble, while Elon Musk responded with a simple "Yikes." Despite these concerns, CoreWeave maintains a $104 billion revenue backlog, and NVIDIA (NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang has defended the company. Meanwhile, Cathie Wood's ARK Invest and Cantor Fitzgerald see opportunity in the sell-off. Eric examines Nebius' financing strategy, CoreWeave's soaring interest expenses, and why declining Treasury yields haven't stopped the bleeding. Are CoreWeave and Nebius bargain-priced AI investments, or is Wall Street uncovering a fundamental weakness in the neocloud business model?

He also compares the Magnificent Seven's performance in 2026 against their remarkable returns since the beginning of 2023, revealing a very different picture of the AI investment boom. items.title: The Next Stock Market Crash Could Start With Just 3 Companies
items.summary: Just three companies now account for approximately 21% of the S&P 500's total market capitalization. NVIDIA (NVDA), Apple (AAPL), and Microsoft (MSFT) have become so dominant that their performance could determine the direction of the entire stock market. But what happens if these technology giants stumble? In this episode, 24/7 Wall St. co-founder Doug McIntyre and senior writer Lee Jackson discuss the extraordinary concentration of the S&P 500 and why millions of investors may be taking on more risk than they realize. Much of today's market enthusiasm is driven by artificial intelligence. Companies like NVIDIA, Microsoft, Alphabet (GOOGL), Amazon (AMZN), and Meta Platforms (META) have benefited from enormous expectations for AI growth. But Doug and Lee identify several potential threats to that optimism. They explore how cheaper open-source AI models could challenge industry leaders, why opposition to AI data center construction threatens expansion plans, and how growing electricity demand is driving renewed interest in nuclear power. Most importantly, they discuss what could happen to popular index funds like the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) if the market's largest technology stocks suffer a major sell-off. They also examine whether equal-weight S&P 500 funds could provide investors with better diversification. Is your S&P 500 investment more vulnerable than you think?

items.title: Elon Musk Has a Tesla Problem He Can’t Seem to Fix
items.summary: Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA) has been one of the most remarkable wealth creators in stock market history. But with Tesla shares falling roughly 20% this year, investors are beginning to ask a difficult question: Has Wall Street finally lost patience with Elon Musk? In this episode, 24/7 Wall St. co-founder Doug McIntyre joins senior writer and editor Lee Jackson to discuss why Tesla is dramatically underperforming many of its Magnificent Seven peers, and whether the company's biggest problem is Elon Musk himself. For years, Musk has argued that Tesla is much more than an electric vehicle manufacturer. He has promised revolutionary advances in artificial intelligence, humanoid robotics, autonomous driving, and robotaxis. Yet many of those promises have taken far longer to materialize than investors expected. Doug explains why Tesla's extraordinary valuation may be increasingly difficult to justify if investors begin treating it primarily as an automotive company rather than an emerging AI powerhouse. The discussion also explores Tesla's electric vehicle sales, its popularity in California, the impact of gasoline prices, growing skepticism surrounding Musk's ambitious timelines, and what upcoming third-quarter earnings could mean for TSLA shareholders. Is Tesla still one of the market's greatest growth stories, or has the Elon Musk premium finally started to disappear?
